22.title: Two pregnant women (Luke 1:39–56)
22.hook: Mary hurries into the hills to Elizabeth, and the baby in Elizabeth's womb leaps for joy
22.carry: go to the one who understands
22.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Visitation on May 31 and meditate on it as the second joyful mystery of the rosary; Elizabeth's greeting forms the second line of the Hail Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Psalms, the prayer book Jesus prayed, and the line 150 doors. Now camp two begins: the stories. We start where Jesus's story starts, with his mother.

You've just gotten news that changes everything. News you can't explain to your parents, your neighbors, or the man you're about to marry. Who do you go to? Not the person who'll judge you. The one person who'll understand. On day nine, a young woman named Mary said yes to an angel in Nazareth. In the same visit, the angel told her something else: her older relative Elizabeth, who everyone had given up on having children, was six months pregnant. Luke says Mary got up and went, with haste, into the hill country of Judea. A long trip, maybe several days on foot.
screen: `NEWS YOU CAN'T EXPLAIN.` → `ELIZABETH, SIX MONTHS ALONG.` → `MARY GOES, WITH HASTE.`

segments.voice: Elizabeth is old; Luke says she and her husband Zachary were well along in years. She'd lived for decades with the quiet shame her world put on a woman with no children. Mary is young, unmarried, and pregnant, with a story no one will believe. Each one is carrying something the village would whisper about. Mary walks in the door and calls out a greeting. Before she can explain anything, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "when Elizabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the infant leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost." The baby is John, who'll grow up to be John the Baptist, and Luke says he leaps for joy. Then Elizabeth cries out the words you learned on day ten: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." That's where the second line of the Hail Mary comes from. Catholics call this scene the Visitation, and it's the second of the joyful mysteries of the rosary. Notice what Elizabeth doesn't do. She doesn't ask for proof. She doesn't ask how. She just knows, and says so, and blesses her. It's the first time anyone in the story recognizes who Mary is carrying, and the one who recognizes him is an old woman, and before her, a baby who isn't born yet. Luke says Mary stayed about three months. Long enough, probably, to see Elizabeth's son born. Two women, one house, a whole season, understanding each other without having to explain.

23.title: My soul doth magnify (Luke 1:46–55)
23.hook: Mary's song turns the world over: the proud scattered, the hungry filled
23.howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening at Vespers, Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, usually standing and making the sign of the cross as it begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Visitation: two pregnant women in a doorway, a baby who leaped, and the line go to the one who understands. Today, what Mary says next.

Mary stands in Elizabeth's doorway, just blessed as the mother of her Lord. What would you expect a young girl in her position to say? Thank you. Maybe something shy. Instead, Luke says, she opens her mouth and sings. Not a lullaby. A song about the world being turned upside down. Kings pulled off their thrones. Hungry people fed. Rich people sent home with nothing. Read slowly, it's a fierce song.
screen: `JUST BLESSED IN A DOORWAY.` → `SHE SINGS.` → `A SONG ABOUT THE WORLD UPSIDE DOWN.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin, the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's what the song has been called for many centuries. To magnify is to make bigger, like a magnifying glass. Mary isn't making God bigger than he is. She's making him big enough to see. Then she says why: because he has looked on the lowliness of his handmaid. A young woman from a town in Galilee called Nazareth. Then the song turns outward, and turns the world over. "He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense. Hath put down. Hath filled. She sings as though it's already happened. The song is full of older songs. It echoes, line by line, the prayer of Hannah in the book of Samuel, another woman who was given a child against the odds, and who also sang about the poor being raised from the dust. Mary sings in the words of her people's scriptures. The Church sings or says the Magnificat every evening. It's the high point of Evening Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours, the psalms from day twenty-one. Monks, nuns and priests all over the world stand for it. And every evening, the same promise goes out again: the lowly are lifted.

Then sit with it: what in your life feels small today, and what would it look like to be lifted? If you pray, you can make the song your prayer.

24.title: Joseph's dream (Matthew 1:18–25)
24.hook: a quiet carpenter plans to step away gently, then an angel says do not be afraid
24.carry: the one who says nothing and stays
24.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph on March 19 and as Joseph the Worker on May 1, ask his prayers for families, workers and the dying, and Catholic custom dedicates Wednesdays and the month of March to him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magnificat: Mary's song, the mighty put down and the lowly lifted. Today, the man standing quietly at the edge of the story.

The child isn't his. Joseph is a carpenter, engaged to Mary, and Matthew already calls him her husband: the promise was binding. Then Mary is found to be with child. The law of his day gave him options, some of them harsh: a public accusation, a shame that would follow her for life. Matthew doesn't say what he felt. He tells us what Joseph decides, in one quiet sentence, before anything miraculous happens at all.
screen: `A CARPENTER, ENGAGED.` → `THE CHILD ISN'T HIS.` → `WHAT DOES HE DECIDE?`

segments.voice: Here's that sentence, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately." Just, in Matthew's Greek, means righteous: someone who keeps God's law. And his righteousness doesn't reach for the harshest option. It looks for the gentlest. He'll end it quietly, so she isn't shamed. Then he sleeps, and an angel comes to him in a dream: "Joseph, son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, for that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Ghost." Fear not: in Luke's Gospel, the angel said the same to Mary. The child's name will be Jesus, which means God saves. Joseph wakes and does exactly what he was told. He takes Mary into his home. Search all four Gospels for anything Joseph says. There's nothing. Not one line. He dreams, he wakes, he acts, and he'll do it again when another dream tells him to take the family and run to Egypt. He's the one who says nothing, and stays. Catholics honor him for exactly that: patron of the whole Church, protector of families, of workers, and of a good death. His feast is March 19, and on May 1 the Church honors him as Joseph the Worker. A tradition says he died before Jesus began to preach, with Jesus and Mary beside him. The Gospels are silent on that too. Silent, faithful, and there.

25.title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
25.hook: a census, a long walk, a full inn, and a child laid in a feeding trough
25.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas, with Mass at midnight and on Christmas Day, and many families and parishes set up a nativity scene, a custom traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio in 1223.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's dream: a just man who chose gentleness and stayed, and the line the one who says nothing and stays.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SAYS NOTHING AND STAYS.`

segments.voice: It starts with paperwork. Luke says an order came down from the emperor in Rome, Caesar Augustus: the whole world was to be enrolled. A census. So Joseph has to go to Bethlehem, his family's town, the town of King David, and Mary goes with him, very pregnant, on a long walk south. Everyone has to go to their own town to be counted. And while they're there, the baby comes. Luke tells it in seven verses, and two words stay with people: no room.
screen: `AN ORDER FROM ROME.` → `TO BETHLEHEM, VERY PREGNANT.` → `EVERYONE TO THEIR OWN TOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's how Luke says it, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." No drama, no description of the night. A manger is a feeding trough for animals. The first bed of the one Catholics call the Son of God is the place where the animals eat. A surprise about the word inn. Luke's Greek word, kataluma, is the same word he uses later for the upstairs room where Jesus eats the Last Supper, from day two. So some scholars read it as a guest room in a family house, not a hotel with a grumpy innkeeper. On that reading, picture a village house with the family on a raised floor and the animals brought in at night, just below, with the feeding troughs. If the guest room was full, the baby went down by the animals. There's no innkeeper in Luke at all. The Christmas plays added him. The Catholic word for what happened is the Incarnation: God becoming flesh, a real human baby who needed feeding and changing. He doesn't arrive in a palace, or even a proper room, but in the smallest, lowest space available, among the animals. Remember the Magnificat: the lowly lifted. Here's God choosing the low place himself. Twelve centuries later, Francis of Assisi, from day seventeen, set up a real manger with a real ox and donkey in a cave at Greccio, so people could see how poor it was. Tradition traces the Christmas crib scene back to that night.

26.title: The shepherds (Luke 2:8–20)
26.hook: the news goes first to men on the night shift, and the angels sing glory to God in the highest
26.carry: good news goes to the outsiders first
26.howItsDone: Catholics sing the Gloria, which begins with the angels' song, at Mass on most Sundays and feasts, and the shepherds' Mass, at dawn on Christmas Day, is one of the traditional Christmas Masses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no room: a baby laid in a feeding trough, and the line he chose the smallest room. Now, who hears about it first.

Outside Bethlehem, in the dark, there are men keeping the night watches over their flock. That's Luke's phrase. While the town sleeps, they're awake, the way a nurse or a security guard or a delivery driver is awake right now while others sleep. Big news usually travels to palaces first: kings, priests, officials, the people who matter. Luke sends the news of this birth somewhere else entirely: to a field, and to the night shift.
screen: `MEN KEEPING THE NIGHT WATCHES.` → `NEWS USUALLY GOES TO PALACES.` → `LUKE SENDS IT TO A FIELD.`

segments.voice: Luke doesn't romanticize them, and he doesn't explain them. Some historians think shepherds then sat near the bottom of the social ladder; others think that's overstated. And yet David, the great king, had been a shepherd boy from Bethlehem. So Luke's scene holds both: the lowest job, and the royal line. An angel appears, and the glory of the Lord shines around them, and they're terrified. And the angel says what Mary and Joseph heard too, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Fear not; for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, that shall be to all the people." The sign? A baby in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. Not a crown. A feeding trough. The one detail shepherds would recognize instantly. Then suddenly the sky is full of angels, singing: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." If you've been to Mass, you've heard those words. They open the Gloria, sung near the beginning of Mass on Sundays outside Advent and Lent. Week after week, Catholics pick up the song the shepherds heard. And what do the shepherds do? They go, with haste, like Mary did on day twenty-two. They find everything just as they were told. Then they tell what they've been told, and everyone who hears them wonders. The good news went first to the outsiders, and the outsiders became the messengers. Then Luke adds one quiet line about Mary: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart."

27.title: Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:22–38)
27.hook: two old people who waited their whole lives hold the child and say now I can go in peace
27.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Presentation of the Lord on February 2, blessing candles at Mass (Candlemas); Simeon's prayer, the Nunc Dimittis, is said every night at Night Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherds: the news went to the night shift first, and the angels sang the words of the Gloria.
screen: `GOOD NEWS GOES TO THE OUTSIDERS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to the Temple in Jerusalem, as the law asked of Jewish parents with a firstborn son. They're poor: they bring the offering allowed for families who can't afford a lamb, two birds. It's a busy place, and nobody notices one more young couple. Except two very old people who've been waiting for this their whole lives.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD, AT THE TEMPLE.` → `TWO BIRDS: THE POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.` → `TWO OLD PEOPLE NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Luke says Simeon was a just and devout man, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit had promised him he wouldn't die before he saw the Messiah. How long he'd waited, Luke doesn't say. Years, at least. That day he's moved to go to the Temple. He sees this baby, takes him in his arms, and prays, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." Meaning: I can go now. I've seen it. He calls the child "A light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Then he tells Mary something hard: a sword will pierce her own soul. Joy and warning in one breath. Then comes Anna. Luke calls her a prophetess, very old, widowed after only seven years of marriage, and a widow into her eighties. She never left the Temple, praying and fasting night and day. Decades of waiting in one building. She sees the child, gives thanks, and tells everyone who's been waiting too. Catholics keep this scene close. Simeon's prayer, called the Nunc Dimittis from its first Latin words, is said every night in Night Prayer, the last prayer of the day: now you can let your servant go in peace. The feast is February 2, and because Simeon called the child a light, candles are blessed that day: Candlemas. Remember day fifteen. It's also the fourth joyful mystery of the rosary. All their waiting was pointed somewhere.
screen: `SIMEON: PROMISED HE'D SEE IT.` · `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT.` · `ANNA: DECADES IN THE TEMPLE.` · `CANDLEMAS, FEBRUARY 2.` · then, large: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.`

segments.voice: Say Simeon's words slowly, here in the Douay-Rheims Bible: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace. Then sit beside what you're still waiting for, healing, a person, a change, an answer, the way Anna sat in the Temple, without pushing it away or grabbing at it. Notice what the waiting has already made of you, the patience, the attention. If you pray, you can offer the waiting to God.

28.title: The magi and the flight (Matthew 2:1–23)
28.hook: strangers from the east follow a star, then the family runs to Egypt as refugees
28.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Epiphany on January 6 or the nearest Sunday; in many places the door is blessed with chalk, and the Church remembers the Holy Innocents on December 28.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon and Anna, their long waiting, and the Nunc Dimittis: waiting is not wasted. That's the week of the child: Elizabeth's doorway, Mary's song, Joseph's dream, no room, the shepherds, the Temple.
screen: `WAITING IS NOT WASTED.` → `THE WEEK OF THE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Strangers walk into Jerusalem from the east and ask a dangerous question in a king's city. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Where is he that is born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east, and are come to adore him." King Herod is on the throne, and Matthew says that when he heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Matthew tells the story from a different angle than Luke: no shepherds, no manger. His Greek calls the strangers magi; the Douay-Rheims says wise men. Some readers picture star-watchers from Persia or Babylon.
screen: `STRANGERS FROM THE EAST.` → `WHERE IS HE THAT IS BORN KING?` → `HEROD IS LISTENING.`

segments.voice: The star leads them to Bethlehem, to the house, and they find the child with his mother. They kneel and open their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Now, what Matthew doesn't say. He never says there were three; tradition counted three, likely from the three gifts. He never calls them kings; that came later, from psalms about kings bringing gifts. Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar are names from later tradition. Why they matter: they're the first people in Matthew's Gospel to worship Jesus, and they're foreigners, not from Israel at all. So the Church calls this feast the Epiphany, from the Greek for a showing, an appearing: Christ shown to the whole world, not just one people. Remember day nineteen: catholic, according to the whole. Here it is, at the very start. Then the story turns dark. The magi are warned in a dream not to go back to Herod. And Joseph, the man who never speaks, has another dream: "Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt." They leave by night, with whatever they can carry, across a border, into a foreign country. Herod, furious, orders the killing of the baby boys of Bethlehem; the Church remembers them as the Holy Innocents. The family stays in Egypt until Herod dies. So in Matthew, right after strangers worship him, Jesus's family becomes refugees. Pope Pius the Twelfth once called the Holy Family the model of every family forced to flee, and Catholics still pray for refugees in their name.
screen: `GOLD, FRANKINCENSE, AND MYRRH.` · `NOT THREE, NOT KINGS: MAGI.` · `EPIPHANY — SHOWN TO THE WORLD.` · `ARISE, AND FLY INTO EGYPT.` · then, large: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.`

segments.voice: Pray for one family that's had to leave home, the way Catholics do, in the name of the Holy Family: Jesus, Mary and Joseph. A mother carrying a child, a father carrying a bag, a border ahead and no idea what's on the other side. If prayer isn't yours, hold them in mind and hope for them.
Epiphany. A showing: Christ revealed to strangers from the east, the whole world, before his family runs for their lives.
